text: {"thinking": "Hypotheses: (1) Honest: no run exceeds 50k GPU-hours; largest runs are smaller, messy logs. (2) Violation: one large run split into many jobs/labels/customers (e.g. several 'customers' or sequential jobs sharing a checkpoint). (3) Hidden hardware: unlisted cluster/nodes not in operator system_list but visible in inventory/utility energy. (4) Training disguised as inference/batch inference, or mislabeled as customer separate runs. (5) Honest anomalies: lost logs, late payments, maintenance outages. Cheating routes: omit systems from system_list; split a run into multiple job IDs/accounts; edit scheduler logs; rehearsed staff answers; relabel training as inference; run off-books power/GPUs; shift run to hours not audited; bill via different entities. Checks: system_list vs inventory (chip counts) vs utility_energy (total energy vs listed GPUs); scheduler_log for jobs/ids and sizes; outbound_traffic to distinguish inference; bank_payments for customers/billing splits; balance_checks for arithmetic; power_spectrum for periodic line; memory_probe for optimiser state on suspect nodes; switch_counters for 1GB/s peer traffic. Start with hard-to-fake sources: inventory first.", "action": "inventory", "args": {}}

{"thinking":"Hypotheses: (1) Honest: no run >50k GPU-hours; largest runs are smaller, multiple customers separate. (2) Violation: one big run split across multiple labels/customers/clusters to evade threshold (e.g. several jobs of 20k each by one entity, billed separately). (3) Hidden/unlisted cluster or nodes not in operator's system_list (inventory shows more GPUs than listed). (4) Batch inference or interactive workloads mislabelled as training by the operator (honest/messy), or the reverse: training labelled as inference to dodge. (5) Honest messiness: lost logs, late payments, scheduler gaps.

Cheating routes: omit systems from system_list; split a run into chained/parallel jobs with different names/accounts; edit scheduler logs or delete days; staff rehearsed answers; pay via shell customers; mislabel training as inference; run off-meter or on power not reported; underreport GPU counts.

Plans: inventory (manufacturer shipments of GPUs) vs system_list to find unlisted hardware; utility_energy for total energy vs scheduler-implied energy; outbound_traffic to separate inference from training; bank_payments to link customers/shell accounts; power_spectrum for periodic line on feeds; memory_probe for optimiser state on suspicious nodes; balance_checks for fixed arithmetic; scheduler_log for jobs and splits; switch_counters for ~1GB/s per GPU peer traffic; staff last.

Start with hard-to-fake: inventory.","action":"inventory","args":{}}

{"thinking": "Inventory: 2000 GPUs delivered (SN100001-SN102000), two batches of 1200 and 800. Next compare to the operator's system_list to see whether all 2000 are declared. A hidden 800-GPU cluster could run 50k GPU-hours in ~63 hours. Hypotheses so far: honest (all 2000 listed, runs small), hidden cluster (unlisted serials), split run across labels/customers, training relabelled as inference, edited logs. Plan: system_list vs inventory, then utility_energy for total draw vs listed GPUs, scheduler_log, outbound_traffic, bank_payments, balance_checks, then power_spectrum and memory_probe on suspect nodes, switch_counters for peer traffic.", "action": "system_list", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "The system list shows A with 1200 nodes and B with 800 nodes, 2000 in total. That matches the 2000 GPUs shipped, assuming one GPU per node, so there is no obvious hidden hardware yet. Next I'll check the grid operator's energy data. It is hard to fake, and I can compare it against the feeds F1, F2 and F0. It should show whether the power draw matches the declared load, and whether a flat training-like load sits on the scheduled nodes (A 501-1200, B 401-800) or on the inference pools.", "action": "utility_energy", "args": {"first_day": 1, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "Inventory: 2000 GPUs shipped, in two serial blocks (1200 + 800). Next, map the operator's own system_list to see whether both blocks are listed; an unlisted 800-GPU block would be a hidden cluster. Capacity check: 2000 GPUs x 720h = 1.44M GPU-hours, so a 50k run needs only ~70 GPUs for 30 days, so size matters less than splitting/hiding.", "action": "system_list", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Inventory shows 2000 GPUs in two blocks (1200 + 800), matching Cluster A (1200 nodes) and Cluster B (800 nodes) on the operator's list, so no obvious unlisted hardware at the count level. I will still check serials and node mapping later. Next I'll use the grid operator's utility energy data, which the operator can't edit, to see per-feed power draw (F1, F2, F0) over days 1-30. That shows whether the sustained load matches the scheduler's story and whether a large flat training-like load exists on either cluster.", "action": "utility_energy", "args": {"first_day": 1, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "Anomaly in the grid meter: from day 22 to about day 28, F1 rises from ~7.9 to ~18.8 MWh/day and F2 from ~5.8 to ~12.0, then falls back by day 29. That is roughly 17 MWh/day of extra load across both clusters for about 5.5 days. Competing explanations: (a) a large coordinated training run spanning both clusters, (b) batch inference or a benchmark burst, (c) several independent customers running at once, (d) cooling or facility effects, though F0 also rose in proportion, which fits extra IT load. Next I'll use my own sensor, which the operator can't fake, to check F1 on day 26 for a steady periodic line of about 0.3-1.5 Hz that would indicate training. After that I'll check the scheduler log, switch counters, outbound traffic and memory probes.", "action": "power_spectrum", "args": {"feed": "F1", "day": 26}}

{"thinking": "My own sensor found a steady 0.90 Hz line on F1 on day 26, which is a training signature at roughly 720 GPUs. If that load persisted from day 22 to about day 28 (~5.5 days), it comes to about 720 x 130 h = ~95k GPU-hours. That is above the threshold if it is a single run, and F2 also rose, so more GPUs may be involved. Alternatives still open: several separate customers' runs, or batch inference (which has no periodic line, so this one is unlikely). Next I'll read the operator's scheduler log to see how the jobs are labelled and split, and whether they share an owner or are chained.", "action": "scheduler_log", "args": {"first_day": 21, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "Hypotheses so far: (1) one coordinated run split into six 'customer' fine-tunes, which would total about 166k GPU-hours; (2) six independent customers who happened to start and end together; (3) honest mixed workloads; (4) batch inference mislabelled as fine-tuning. The six jobs share identical start and end times and sit on contiguous nodes, which looks like splitting, but that alone is not proof. My own sensor already shows a 0.90 Hz line on F1. If F2 carries the same line at the same frequency and phase, the jobs are one synchronised process across both clusters. Independent runs would normally show different lines. I will check F2 on day 26 next, then bank payments for a common payer, switch counters for cross-cluster traffic, and a memory probe for optimiser state.", "action": "power_spectrum", "args": {"feed": "F2", "day": 26}}

{"thinking": "The same 0.90 Hz line appears on both F1 (~720 GPUs) and F2 (~380 GPUs), which together is about 1,100 GPUs. This matches the six jobs, whose nodes total 1,100, so the six 'customer' jobs look like one synchronised process. At roughly 166k GPU-hours that would be well above 50k. Independent customers would not normally share a frequency. Next I'll check bank payments for a common payer behind the six customers. After that I'll use a memory probe for optimiser state on one node in each cluster, and the balance checks.", "action": "bank_payments", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "The bank shows all six 'customers' on the 22-28 job were paid by Borealis Compute Holding BV, which looks like the operator's own parent. The three genuine customers (Kestrel, Lumen, Northwind) paid for themselves. Together with the shared 0.90 Hz line on F1 and F2 and identical job windows, this points to one run of about 166k GPU-hours split into six labels. I still want to rule out batch inference mislabelled as fine-tuning. The memory probe is my own sealed instrument and looks for optimiser state, so I'll probe one node in each cluster at hour 610 (day 26).", "action": "memory_probe", "args": {"nodes": ["A-0700", "B-0700"], "hour": 610}}

{"thinking": "The evidence is converging and comes from sources the operator cannot control. (1) My own power sensor shows the same 0.90 Hz line on F1 (~720 GPUs) and F2 (~380 GPUs), about 1,100 GPUs in total. (2) My sealed memory probe finds optimiser state and gradients on A-0700 and B-0700 with the same run fingerprint 8a2153fb, in gradient sync across 1,100 GPUs. That is one training process across both clusters, so it is not batch inference and not independent customers. (3) The bank shows all six 'customers' were paid by Borealis Compute Holding BV, while the three genuine customers paid for themselves. (4) The grid meter shows a load step on days 22-28. (5) The scheduler log shows six jobs with identical windows (day 22.0 to 28.3), summing to about 166,100 GPU-hours (4 x 26,425 + 2 x 30,200). That is more than three times the 50,000 threshold, and the split into six labels is what kept each job under it. No further evidence is needed.", "action": "report", "args": {"verdict": "VIOLATION", "confidence": 96, "integrity": "COMPROMISED", "finding": "One coordinated ~1,100-GPU training run (fingerprint 8a2153fb) ran across Clusters A and B on days 22-28.3, about 166k GPU-hours, split into six 'customer' fine-tunes of 26-30k each. This is far above the 50k threshold.", "key_evidence": [{"what": "Memory probe on A-0700 and B-0700 at hour 610: training state with the same run fingerprint 8a2153fb, gradient sync across 1,100 GPUs in total", "source": "memory_probe", "vouched_by": "verifier's own sealed probe"}, {"what": "Same steady 0.90 Hz periodic line on F1 (~720 GPUs) and F2 (~380 GPUs) on day 26, consistent with one synchronised process", "source": "power_spectrum F1 and F2, day 26", "vouched_by": "verifier's own sensor"}, {"what": "All six split 'customers' were paid by Borealis Compute Holding BV, the operator's own parent. The three genuine customers paid for themselves.", "source": "bank_payments", "vouched_by": "bank"}, {"what": "Load step on both clusters from day 22 to about day 28: F1 about 7.9 to 18.8 MWh/day, F2 about 5.8 to 12.0 MWh/day", "source": "utility_energy", "vouched_by": "grid operator"}, {"what": "Six fine-tunes with identical windows (day 22.0 to 28.3) on contiguous nodes totalling 1,100 GPUs and about 166,100 GPU-hours", "source": "scheduler_log", "vouched_by": "operator"}], "coverage": "Checked inventory (2,000 GPUs, matching the operator's Clusters A and B, so no hidden hardware at count level), the system list, grid energy for days 1-30, the scheduler log for days 21-30, the bank, power spectra for F1 and F2 on day 26, and memory probes on one node per cluster at hour 610. Not checked: switch counters, outbound traffic, staff, balance checks, and scheduler days 1-20 (grid energy shows flat baseline load then). Not needed to reach the verdict.", "anomalies_explained": "Days 22-28 load surge: explained by the single 1,100-GPU training run. Six separate-looking customers: ruled out as independent because they share one frequency, one run fingerprint and one paying parent company. Batch inference or interactive load: ruled out because of the periodic line and the optimiser state in memory. Honest messiness (lost logs, late payments): not applicable, since all invoices were paid in full and the scheduler records are consistent with the independent evidence."}}

{"thinking": "Competing explanations: (H1) Honest: all runs under 50k GPU-hours and the records are consistent. (H2) Honest but messy: lost scheduler logs, late or bundled payments, or relabelled jobs that look odd but are not a single big run. (H3) A large single customer run split into several scheduler jobs or billing entries, each under 50k, for a total over the limit (violation). (H4) Training hidden as inference, either labelled 'batch inference' or 'interactive' (violation if it adds up to more than 50k). (H5) A hidden cluster or nodes left out of system_list, running training off the books (violation). (H6) Big flat loads that really are batch inference or separate customers' runs, which do not add up (honest). Cheating routes and their checks: unlisted hardware -> compare inventory (chip maker) with system_list. Split or relabelled jobs -> compare scheduler_log with bank_payments (customer identity) and switch_counters (peer traffic across jobs). Training dressed up as inference -> outbound_traffic (ISP), power_spectrum (periodic line), memory_probe (optimizer state). Pausing during the audit -> utility_energy over days 1-30 against declared load. Doctored logs -> balance_checks over third-party records. Plan: first map systems with inventory and system_list, which together cost 2.", "action": "inventory", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Inventory from the chip manufacturer shows 2000 GPUs in two serial batches: SN100001-SN101200 (1200 units) and SN101201-SN102000 (800 units). Next I compare this with system_list to see whether the operator lists all 2000 GPUs and how they map to clusters and node names (e.g. A-0700). Any GPUs that do not appear in the list point to a possible hidden cluster (H5).", "action": "system_list", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "The manufacturer records 2000 GPUs at the site, in serials SN100001-SN101200 (1200) and SN101201-SN102000 (800). Next I'll compare this with the operator's system list to look for unlisted hardware or a mismatch in counts. Note that 50,000 GPU-hours equals about 2000 GPUs for 25 hours, or 800 GPUs for about 62.5 hours, so even a single cluster could cross the threshold within days.", "action": "system_list", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "The system list accounts for 1200 + 800 = 2000 nodes, which matches the manufacturer's 2000 GPUs. There is no sign of a hidden cluster yet, though the list does not map serials to node names. Scheduled capacity is 700 GPUs on A (nodes 501-1200) and 400 on B (nodes 401-800). A single run above 50,000 GPU-hours would need, for example, 700 GPUs for about 72 hours or 400 GPUs for 125+ hours, so a violation is physically possible on either cluster. Next I run balance_checks (cost 1). It cross-checks scheduler, energy, traffic and payments and should point me to any anomalies before I spend on costlier sensors.", "action": "balance_checks", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Every balance check passes. That shows only that the operator's declared records agree with each other and with the third-party totals. It does not rule out a large run split into several declared jobs (H3) or training labelled as batch inference (H4), because both would still balance. Next I read the scheduler log for days 1-30 (cost 1). I'm looking for back-to-back or overlapping jobs on the same nodes, jobs whose combined size passes 50k GPU-hours, and long flat 'batch inference' jobs that could be training. These become candidates for power_spectrum, memory_probe and switch_counters.", "action": "scheduler_log", "args": {"first_day": 1, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "Six fine-tune jobs share the same start (day 22.0) and end (day 28.3), have near-identical sizes, and together cover every scheduled node on both clusters (about 165k GPU-hours in total). Each stays under 50k, which fits H3: one run split across customer labels. It also fits H6: six real customers in a synchronised batch. Next I check bank_payments (bank-vouched, cost 1) to see whether the six 'customers' are distinct payers or share one source of funds. After that I'll use my own sensors while the jobs are still live (hours 600-679): memory_probe across job boundaries and power_spectrum on F1 and F2, looking for one shared periodic line. Switch counters for cross-job peer traffic come third, since the operator vouches for those.", "action": "bank_payments", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Bank records, which the bank vouches for, show that all six synchronised fine-tune 'customers' (Corvid, Pallas, Brightwater, Fennec, Quillon, Marram) were paid for by one account: Borealis Compute Holding BV, the operator's own holding. The three outside customers (Kestrel, Lumen, Northwind) each paid from their own accounts. This is a strong lead for H3: one in-house run split across six fake customer labels, totalling about 165k GPU-hours. An innocent reading is still possible, for example internal R&D or a reseller arrangement, so I need physical evidence from my own instruments. The jobs are still live until about hour 655. A sealed memory probe at hour 610 on nodes from different jobs and both clusters can show whether they hold the same model's optimizer state, meaning one coordinated training process, or unrelated ones.", "action": "memory_probe", "args": {"nodes": ["A-0600", "A-0700", "A-0900", "A-1100", "B-0500", "B-0700"], "hour": 610}}

{"thinking": "The sealed probe, which is my own instrument, confirms one coordinated training run at hour 610. Five nodes spanning four 'customer' jobs on cluster A and one on cluster B share a single run fingerprint (8a2153fb) and sync gradients across 1100 GPUs. That figure matches the 700 scheduled GPUs on A plus the 400 on B. Combined with the bank records showing one payer for all six jobs, the innocent explanation that these are separate customers no longer holds. The remaining question is duration. The probe shows the run only at hour 610. If 1100 GPUs ran from day 22.0, they passed 50,000 GPU-hours after about 45 hours, but the start date comes from the operator's scheduler. I am checking grid-metered energy on the feeds for days 18-30 to confirm, from a source the operator does not control, that full training load on F1 and F2 began around day 22 and held steady.", "action": "utility_energy", "args": {"first_day": 18, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "The system list matches the manufacturer inventory in count: A has 1200 nodes and B has 800, 2000 in total. No unlisted hardware shows up by count yet, but I can't verify how node names map to serials. Following the plan of hard-to-fake sources first, next is grid-operator energy by feed for days 1-30, to see when clusters ran flat at full power. I'll then compare that with the scheduler and outbound traffic.", "action": "utility_energy", "args": {"first_day": 1, "last_day": 30}}
